questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real question to ask about any action inside a playbook?
options: Can this action technically be scripted at all?
Is this action low-risk and well-understood enough that being wrong costs very little?
Will this action make the playbook run faster?
Does Azure Logic Apps support this connector?
questions.explain: Almost anything can be automated technically — the real question is whether being wrong about it is cheap or expensive.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a low-risk action that's generally safe to fully automate?
options: Disabling a user's account
Isolating a production server
Tagging an incident as "auto-notified"
Blocking a sender domain organization-wide
questions.explain: Tagging is reversible and purely organizational — exactly the kind of cheap-to-be-wrong-about action safe to automate.

questions.q: Why is disabling a user account typically kept as a human-approved action rather than fully automated?
options: Because Sentinel has no connector capable of disabling accounts
Because it's a low-impact, easily reversible action
Because it's devastating if it turns out to be a false positive against a legitimate user
Because disabling accounts is always the wrong response, even to a confirmed compromise
questions.explain: The action is correct for a confirmed compromise but costly if the detection is wrong, which is why it usually needs an approval step.

questions.q: What does an "approval step" inside a playbook do?
options: Deletes the incident if no one responds within an hour
Automatically approves every action without any review
Pauses the playbook so a human must approve a consequential action before it runs
Replaces the automation rule's condition entirely
questions.explain: The playbook still automates the cheap, low-risk steps, but pauses before the expensive, hard-to-reverse one for human sign-off.

questions.q: What is the practical pattern this lesson recommends for playbook design?
options: Never automate anything — every action should always require manual approval
Automate only actions that involve sending email notifications
Automate the cheap, reversible, high-confidence parts; have a human approve the expensive, hard-to-reverse part
Automate every single action in every playbook with no exceptions
questions.explain: The lesson's pattern splits a playbook: automation handles low-risk steps, approval gates the high-impact one.
